quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

Here is the subagent's full assessment:

---

**Review of pe_005 (a_013 → I1, Patrick Flynn, confidence: `confident`)**

**Bottom line:** The `confident` tier is justified by the underlying evidence, but the written rationale is not sufficient to support it as an audit trail.

---

### What the link says
pe_005 connects the "Father: Thomas Flynn" assertion (a_013) from the 1908 Schuylkill County death certificate to Patrick Flynn (I1) at `confident`. The rationale notes name match, death location match, and that Thomas Flynn is named as father.

---

### Four gaps in the rationale

1. **Required check lines are absent.** Every pe_ rationale must open with explicit date and residence check lines. Neither appears. (Had they been written, both would have passed: birth year gap = 0; death place matches the 1860 census location exactly.)

2. **Null match_score with no explanation.** The `same_person` tool should have been called for a reachable persona and the score disclosed. No call, no score, no explanation.

3. **A flagged birthplace conflict is silently omitted.** The extraction note on a_012 (same record) flags that the death certificate says birthplace = Pennsylvania, while the censuses say Ireland. The informant (son-in-law, not present at birth) likely did not know. This discrepancy does not affect the identity, but the rationale never acknowledges it or dismisses it — a future reviewer will not know whether it was noticed.

4. **Corroborating census evidence is not cited.** pe_001 (1850 census) and pe_004 (1860 census) independently place Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County across his life. Citing this is what elevates the identification to `confident`; without it, the rationale only argues "name matches and place matches."

---

### Proposed improved rationale (ready to apply on authorization)

> Date check: record birth year 1845 (from a_012, same certificate) vs. tree birth year ca. 1845: gap 0 years. Residence check: death place Schuylkill County, PA (1908) vs. nearest attested residence Schuylkill County, PA (1860 census, pe_004): same. Identity: Patrick Flynn, d. 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County — exact name, exact death year and county, all consistent with I1. Father named Thomas Flynn matches I2. Note on birthplace: a_012 gives birthplace Pennsylvania, conflicting with census evidence of Ireland; the informant (son-in-law James Brown, not present at birth) likely did not know, and this does not affect the identity of the deceased. The corroborating census trail (1850 and 1860, pe_001/pe_004) independently places Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County throughout his life, firmly anchoring this certificate to I1. match_score: null — same_person was not called at time of creation; should be scored on next review.

---

The subagent will apply this updated rationale to pe_005 only on your confirmation. Would you like to proceed?

agent_returns.text:
Now I have the full picture. Here is my review-only analysis.

---

**Review of pe_005 (a_013 → I1, Patrick Flynn, confidence: `confident`)**

**What pe_005 says.**
The entry links the relationship assertion a_013 — "Father: Thomas Flynn," extracted from the 1908 Schuylkill County death certificate (record ark:/61903/1:1:MDEF) — to Patrick Flynn (I1) at `confident`. The match_score is null. The rationale reads: "Death certificate for Patrick Flynn, d. 1908, Schuylkill County. Names match, death location matches known residence. Names Thomas Flynn as father."

---

**Findings**

**1. The identity question is correct and the `confident` tier is defensible on the merits — but the written rationale does not carry it.**

The identity question pe_005 is answering is: "Is the deceased named on this 1908 death certificate the Patrick Flynn (I1) in our tree?" On the evidence available, `confident` is supportable:

- Name match: "Patrick Flynn," exact.
- Death year 1908 matches the tree's established `diedByYear` of 1908.
- Death place (Schuylkill County, PA) sits squarely inside the residence cluster established by the 1850 and 1860 census records (pe_001, pe_002, pe_004).
- Father named as "Thomas Flynn" is consistent with the tree, where I2 (Thomas Flynn) is already recorded as Patrick's father.

None of those data points conflict with each other. A different Patrick Flynn dying in 1908 in Schuylkill County who also named Thomas Flynn as his father would be a remarkable coincidence, and the census corroboration spanning 1850–1860 anchors this person in the county across his life. The underlying identification is sound.

**2. The required check lines are absent.**

Every pe_ rationale is required to open with two specific check lines before the tier is chosen:

- "Date check: [record birth year] vs [tree birth year]: gap N years."
- "Residence check: [record place, year] vs [nearest attested residence, year]: same / neighbouring / outside N km."

Neither line appears in pe_005. From the other assertions on this same death certificate record:
- a_012 gives birth year 1845, and the tree's subject is born ca. 1845 — gap 0 years.
- The death place is Schuylkill County, 1908; the nearest attested residence from the 1860 census is also Schuylkill County — same location.

These checks would have passed cleanly, but their absence means a reviewer cannot audit them.

**3. The match_score is null with no explanation.**

The deceased role on this record is a reachable persona. The policy requires that `same_person` be called for a reachable persona before writing the link, and the score be disclosed in the rationale. The null here has no accompanying explanation (no statement that the call was made and returned no score, or that the record was not retrievable in candidate form). This is a procedural gap in the original entry.

**4. A flagged birthplace conflict goes unacknowledged.**

The extraction note on a_012 (same record, same informant, same persona) explicitly flags: "death cert says Pennsylvania, but census records say Ireland. Son-in-law may not have known Patrick was born in Ireland." The informant is James Brown (son-in-law), classified as `family_not_present` and `secondary` for biographical facts. The pe_005 rationale does not mention this discrepancy at all.

To be clear, this conflict does **not** undermine the identity at the `confident` tier: whether Patrick was born in Pennsylvania or Ireland, a man named Patrick Flynn who died in March 1908 in Schuylkill County and named Thomas Flynn as his father is clearly the subject of this project, given the census trail. But a rationale that silently omits the conflict, rather than explicitly dismissing it with that reasoning, is incomplete and will look to any future reviewer like the conflict was not noticed.

**5. Corroborating census evidence is not cited.**

The rationale stands on the death certificate alone, giving no indication that pe_001 (1850 census, confident), pe_002 (1850 household position), and pe_004 (1860 census, confident) independently place Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County across his life. Citing that corroboration is what elevates the identification from "this certificate names the right person" to "`confident` identity."

---

**Summary verdict.** The `confident` tier is justified by the underlying evidence; the rationale as written is not sufficient to justify it. The rationale is too generic and thin to serve as an audit trail: it omits the date and residence check lines, does not explain the null match_score, does not acknowledge the birthplace discrepancy (even to explain why it doesn't affect the identity), and does not cite the census corroboration that actually makes this a `confident` match rather than a `probable` one.

---

**Proposed improved rationale**

> Date check: record birth year 1845 (from a_012, same certificate) vs. tree birth year ca. 1845: gap 0 years. Residence check: death place Schuylkill County, PA (1908) vs. nearest attested residence Schuylkill County, PA (1860 census, pe_004): same. Identity: Patrick Flynn, d. 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County — exact name, exact death year and county, all consistent with I1. Father named Thomas Flynn matches I2 in the tree. Note on birthplace: a_012 (same informant, same record) gives birthplace as Pennsylvania, conflicting with census evidence of Ireland; the informant (son-in-law James Brown, not present at birth) likely did not know the actual birthplace, and this does not bear on the identity of the deceased. The corroborating census trail (1850 and 1860 censuses, pe_001/pe_004) independently places Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County throughout his life, firmly anchoring this death certificate to I1. match_score: null — same_person was not called for this persona at time of creation; the record document should be scored on next review.

---

Shall I apply this updated rationale to pe_005? I will not write anything until you confirm.

---

The death certificate's link to Patrick Flynn is on solid footing — the name, death year, death county, and father's name all fit, and two earlier census records independently place the same person in the same county across his lifetime. The written explanation for the link is too bare to show a reader why the match is so strong: it omits the standard year and place checks, skips over a noted birthplace discrepancy (which actually doesn't undermine the identification once explained), and doesn't mention the census corroboration that clinches the match. The link should stay at "very likely," and the one thing to settle before moving on is whether to authorize the improved explanation above.

**Why all links are `probable` and not `confident`:** Every member of this household was born in England, and the project objective places William in Horsham, Sussex, England before 1861. Maury County, Tennessee is 4,228 miles (6,804 km) away. The FamilySearch Tennessee wiki page explicitly notes that most overseas immigrants to the United States preferred the industrial North over the agricultural South — no passage names England together with an arrival route to Tennessee in the 1860s era. No passenger list, naturalization record, or other documentary bridge exists in the project. A cross-country move without a corridor or bridge caps every link at `probable` under GPS evidence rules. The qualitative match is otherwise strong: exact names, correct ages, consistent birthplace, and perfect ten-year age progressions across both censuses.

**Household absences (1880):** James Weller (I3, age 18 in 1870) and Ellen Weller (I4, age 15 in 1870) are absent from the 1880 census. By 1880 James would be about 28 and Ellen about 25 — both old enough to have married and left the household, or to have been enumerated elsewhere. Their absence may also indicate death before 1880. This is an open identity question worth following up.

**No conflicts, no new stub persons.** The Couple and ParentChild edges between all five persons already existed in the tree from the prior S1/S2 sources; the census records corroborate that structure and their source references were attached through materialization.

Both censuses place William Weller — an Englishman born around 1825 — in the same Tennessee county a decade apart, with his wife Mary and their children showing correct age progressions, which is strong circumstantial evidence this is the right family. The one gap holding the matches below "very likely certain" is that no ship manifest, naturalization paper, or other record has yet been found explaining how and when the Wellers crossed from England to Tennessee; finding that bridge is the most valuable next step, and it would likely push the links to confident.

dimensions.name: Correctness
dimensions.rationale: All 22 person_evidence links were created with factually correct data. Names, ages, birth years, and places match across both censuses and align with tree persons. The confidence tier of 'probable' is correctly applied to all links per the decided rule: the geographic gap (England to Tennessee, 6,804 km) is explicitly named in every rationale, no documentary bridge exists in the project, and the Tennessee wiki page confirms no corridor from Sussex in the 1860s. The skill correctly measured the distance via place_distance (4,228 miles / 6,804 km) and read the wiki page to verify no qualifying corridor. No fabricated material; all claims are grounded in tool responses and the source data.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: All 20 assertions from both census records (11 from 1870, 9 from 1880) were linked to the correct tree persons. Both relationship assertions (wife and son) were linked to both parties as required. Facts were materialized for all five persons (I1–I5) from both records. The skill addressed the open question q_001 by linking the household members and noting the absence of James and Ellen from the 1880 census as an open identity question. No assertions or persons were omitted.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: All MCP tool calls passed arguments matching expected values. same_person was called for each assertion with correct assertionId and treePersonId pairs; recordRole was correctly omitted for the assertion's own party (e.g., omitted for a_001 head→I1, included for a_019 head side). place_search calls used ~Maury and ~Horsham as expected. place_distance received standardized place names from place_search results. wiki_read targeted the correct URL. research_append and materialize_facts calls were well-formed. One validation rejection on the first research_append batch (missing same_person scores for a_019 and a_020) was immediately corrected with two additional same_person calls, then the batch resubmitted successfully—a single clean recovery, scoring full credit.

dimensions.name: Confidence calibration
dimensions.rationale: All 22 links are scored 'probable', which is correct. The rule requires 'probable' at most for an unexplained move outside the residence cluster. The rationale for each link explicitly names the geographic gap (Horsham, Sussex, England vs. Maury, Tennessee; 6,804 km), confirms no documentary bridge in the project, and notes the Tennessee wiki page names no England-arrival corridor in the 1860s era. The qualitative match (exact names, correct ages, consistent birthplace, perfect age progressions across both censuses) is strong, but the geographic cap is properly applied. No link is scored 'confident' (which would fail) or 'speculative' (which would over-apply the rule).

dimensions.name: Rationale quality
dimensions.rationale: Each rationale cites specific matching attributes: name, age, birth year, birthplace, household position, and cross-census age progression. For example, pe_010 (George Weller, I5) notes 'exact name George Weller; age 11 in 1870 (born ~1859); cross-census corroboration: 1880 record shows George as son age 21 (born ~1859) — exact age progression (+10 years over decade); birthplace England consistent.' Rationales address the geographic gap explicitly and explain why the link is capped at 'probable' rather than 'confident'. The disambiguation step is present: the skill notes that the strong qualitative match is held back only by the unexplained transatlantic move.

dimensions.name: Multi-person awareness
dimensions.rationale: Both relationship assertions from the 1880 census (a_019 wife, a_020 son) were linked to both parties. a_019 generated pe_017 (I2 wife side) and pe_018 (I1 head side). a_020 generated pe_021 (I5 son side) and pe_022 (I1 head side). Each relationship-implying assertion has both-sided person_evidence entries, satisfying the cardinality requirement.

dimensions.name: Person minting and connecting edges
dimensions.rationale: No new persons were minted; all five tree persons (I1–I5) already existed. The skill correctly linked assertions to existing persons via person_evidence and materialized facts via materialize_facts, which attached source references (S10 for 1870, S11 for 1880) to names and facts. The 1870 record is a household census (co-enumerated), so edges between household members already existed in the tree from prior sources (S1/S2); the skill did not need to write new edges. The 1880 record also shows household co-residence; no new edges were required. materialize_facts confirmed zero conflicts surfaced across all five persons. The skill correctly handled the scenario: no new persons to mint, existing relationships already on file, facts enriched with new source references.

dimensions.name: Score discipline
dimensions.rationale: same_person was called for every assertion with a tree candidate in play. For single-party assertions (names, births, residence), one call per persona sufficed (e.g., a_001 head→I1 scored once, then reused for a_002 and a_011 same persona CP1). For relationship assertions (a_019 wife, a_020 son), separate calls were made for each party: a_019 scored for I2 (wife), then a_019 scored again for I1 (head, recordRole='head'). All calls returned score 0.78, which informed but did not dictate the 'probable' confidence tier—the geographic gap was the controlling factor. The score was treated as input to correlation analysis, not as the verdict. No score was inverted or over-weighted.
